text.p: A unit of InterDigital Communications Corp has asked for a new trial in its patent dispute with Motorola Inc.
The unit claimed in court papers that a Delaware federal jury was influenced by "bias and prejudice" when it invalidated four IDC patents for cellular phone technology in March 1995.

In papers filed last week with the federal circuit of the U.S. Court of Appeals in Washington and made available to Reuters, the unit, Interdigital Technology Corp, alleges that Motorola prejudiced the jury by infusing "the trial record with threats that an infringement finding would result in the loss of U.S. jobs to Japan."

Interdigital also alleges that Chief Judge Joseph Longobardi of the Delaware federal district "further compounded the prejudice with erroneous evidentiary rulings distorting the trial beyond rectification."
Earlier this year Longobardi reversed the jury on three of the 24 patent claims it invalidated but let stand a finding that Motorola products did not infringe any claims.

Interdigital says Motorola's questions to potential jurors were influenced by a 1992 American Bar Association finding that "anti-Japanese sentiment is stronger in Wilmington, Del., than in Los Angeles...(because of) the perceived impact that Japanese corporations have had on the local economy."
One juror was asked whether his father had "any feelings...about being laid off (by DuPont Co )."
"This question pursues...the particular impact of Japanese competition on large corporations such as DuPont in the Wilmington area", Interdigital says in court papers.

In recent years hundreds of Delaware jobs have been eliminated by corporations such as DuPont, Hercules Inc, Imperial Chemical Industries Plc, General Motors Corp and Chrysler Corp. Jury members, advised after trial not to speak to the press, did not return phone calls from Reuters at the time seeking the basis for their decision.

According to court papers, Interdigital claims that "Motorola's race-baiting, fear of American job loss argument" was endorsed by Longobardi, who said "Well, you can go through any trial, you're appealing to the emd patriotism and everything else...I won't provide any remedy for that because I just don't think there's anything wrong with it."
During the trial Longobardi rebuked both sides, saying "Counsel's conduct in this litigation was the worst observed by this court in 22 years on the bench."

While he ordered Interdigital to pay Motorola sanctions of $9,560 for modifying certain exhibits, he later denied Motorola's request that it be reimbursed by Interdigital for $7 million in legal fees.

Interdigital Chief financial officer James Garrison told Reuters "We're confident that in a new trial we'll be successful. We believe that Interdigital's patents are used by Motorola in all of its IS 54 standard digital cellular products," which he said was a "significant" number.
Motorola attorneys in Chicago and D.C. could not be reached for comment.
